title: Streaming latency ripple postmortem
content:
SUMMARY

What happened (tl;dr): On 2029-05-02 between ~17:10 and 17:38 UTC we experienced a multi-region streaming latency regression that manifested as long tail (p95-p999) increases and client-observed stalls/reconnects for hosted API streaming sessions. No broad increase in request rate was observed; the incident correlates with a small but repeated set of KV cache invalidations for high-prefix keys which triggered an expensive KV prefetch path and introduced transient GPU memory pressure and scheduler stall in the serving runtime. The result: streaming chunks delayed by dozens to hundreds of ms, several sessions timed out and clients retried, pushing backpressure into edge multiplexers and briefly increasing 502/503s on a small percentage of requests.

Customer impact: P0 severity for a subset of customers using long-running streaming sessions (chat widgets, realtime transcription connectors). Estimated affected sessions: ~6k concurrent sessions across two regions at peak. Errors: ~1.2% additional 5xx for streaming endpoints during the window, primarily 502/503 from edge timeouts and 504s from upstream stall detectors. Several customer on-call pages and SRE alerts were triggered.

Detection: Alerts fired first at 17:16 UTC for p99 streaming latency > 2s in us-west1. Pager rotation started 17:18 UTC. On-call noticed increased reconnect traces and streaming reassembly TTL warnings.

TIMELINE (UTC)

- 17:09:40 - subtle metric drift: KV cache invalidation rate for prefix /v1/streams/prefix-A increased from baseline ~0.1/min to ~1.3/min (an automated rollout introduced invalidation on a small subset).
- 17:12:05 - edge multiplexer observed slowwrite backpressure on connections destined for runtime pool r-azure-gpu-6. Alerts not yet firing.
- 17:15:30 - synthetic and real-user p99 streaming latency crosses 2s in us-west1, alerting rule fires.
- 17:16:40 - SRE on-call paged; triage begins. Initial hypothesis: upstream autoscaler oscillation.
- 17:18:10 - traces show increased durations in kernel that handles KV prefetch and KV deserialization at runtime host; single-request token generation timeouts observed.
- 17:21:02 - manual rollback of the small invalidation rollout (feature flag toggle) started; invalidation events drop but residual pressure remains due to concurrent prefetch and in-progress evictions.
- 17:26:30 - first customer-visible reconnects recorded; edge returns 502 for some streaming resumptions.
- 17:32:00 - runtime memory usage shows transient spike and higher GC/cleanup latencies; scheduler logs show stalls waiting on prefetched KV deserialization locks.
- 17:36:00 - mitigation step: degrade prefetch path to synchronous shallow-load (cheap path) by flipping a runtime switch; observed p99 drop.
- 17:38:10 - user-visible metrics normalized for most sessions; follow-on cleanup and telemetry collection continues.

ROOT CAUSE

Primary cause: A controlled invalidation rollout (targeted to a small traffic slice) inadvertently created a repeated invalidation pattern for a hot key prefix. The runtime's aggressive KV prefetch logic attempted to prefetch many adjacent cache entries in parallel to reduce downstream latency. In this workload the prefetch combined with concurrent evictions and deserialization caused increased GPU memory pressure and scheduler stalls — in turn delaying token emission for active streaming sessions. The delay cascaded: clients hit SDK-side timeouts and tried reconnects, edge multiplexer experienced bursts, and some requests returned 502/503 prior to autoscaler or circuit-breaker giving way.

Contributing factors:
- KV prefetch path is optimistic and parallel by default; lacks a per-prefix concurrency limiter.
- Runtime lock acquisition for KV deserialization is coarse-grained and can block other lightweight tasks.
- The invalidation rollout was not gated by an additional chaos window or canary traffic ramp that would detect instability in streaming workloads.
- Edge/multiplex layer backpressure metrics are hard to correlate to prefetch pressure currently (no single dashboard).
- Some streaming clients use short resume timeouts which cause immediate reconnects rather than gracefully waiting through microbursts.

DETECTION & RESPONSE

What alerted us: p99 streaming latency rule and client reconnect spikes.
What we did first:
- Triage: confirmed it's streaming-only, not batch generation.
- Scoped: narrowed to a specific prefix and runtime pool using traces.
- Immediate action: toggled feature flag to stop issuing new invalidations to the hot prefix (17:21).
- Short mitigation: disabled aggressive prefetch by enabling the shallow-load runtime switch (17:36).
- Communication: incident channel opened, CS notified, status page updated with limited impact notice.

Why response took time:
- The pressure was produced by in-flight prefetch tasks already scheduled; stopping new invalidations helped but did not immediately drain prefetches.
- Observability gap: KV prefetch queue depth and per-prefix concurrency were not surfaced in the main streaming dashboard, which slowed root-cause confirmation.

MITIGATIONS & REMEDIATION

Immediate (done during incident):
- Rolled back invalidation rollout for the prefix (feature flag).
- Toggled runtime to synchronous shallow-load prefetch mode to avoid parallel heavy deserialization.
- Cleared an edge multiplexer backlog by temporarily increasing connection worker count for affected pools (short-term).

Short-term (next 1–2 weeks):
- Add per-prefix prefetch concurrency throttle in runtime with default conservative limits.
- Add a dashboard showing KV prefetch queue depth, per-prefix invalidation rate, and deserialization lock contention metrics.
- Add alerting for rapid increases in invalidation rate for hot prefixes (>0.5/min sustained) with severity-level mapping.
- Update rollout checklist to include streaming workload canary gate and explicit monitoring for key prefixes used by streaming.

Medium-term (1–3 months):
- Rework KV deserialization locks to be finer-grained or use lock-free deserialization where possible.
- Implement prefetch backpressure signals to edge/multiplex layer so it can shed or smooth streaming resumption attempts.
- Add a runtime knob to auto-fallback to tokenized prefix-only path for long-running streaming sessions when prefetch pressure is detected.

Long-term (3–6 months):
- Explore inserting a lightweight streaming-side circuit (per-session) that allows graceful pacing and reduces client reconnect loops.
- Consider redesign so invalidation rollouts auto-throttle based on detected runtime prefetch/backpressure signals.

ACTION ITEMS (owner -> due)

- "Add per-prefix prefetch concurrency throttle" -> Marco Chen -> 2029-05-10
- "Dashboard: KV prefetch queue + prefix invalidation rate" -> Evelyn Park -> 2029-05-09
- "Rollout checklist update: streaming canary gate" -> Diego Alvarez -> 2029-05-06
- "Runtime: shallow-lock/deserialization work plan" -> Priya Rao -> 2029-06-15
- "Incident blameless write-up and customer FAQ" -> Samira Khatri -> 2029-05-05

RUNBOOK UPDATES (notes to self)

- Add a new runbook section: "Streaming: KV-prefetch pressure" with play actions:
  - Check prefix invalidation rate (prod-metrics.kv.invalidation_rate_by_prefix)
  - If >0.5/min for hot prefix, flip feature flag to pause invalidations for that prefix and throttle prefetch (if runtime switch exists)
  - If p99 streaming latency > 2s and prefetch queue depth rising, set runtime to shallow-load prefetch mode and scale connection workers on edge multiplexers
  - If reconnect spike >3x baseline, coordinate with CS to set status page to degraded and open customer-facing channel

- Add exact CLI commands and path to feature flag toggle in next patch. Also capture the runtime switch name used during this incident (prefetch.mode=shallow-sync).

COMMUNICATION

- Internal: Incident channel (#inc-5421) created; full notes posted.
- External: Customer-facing note posted to status page indicating degraded streaming for a subset of customers between 17:15–17:38 UTC. CS follow-up: outreach to top affected customers.

LESSONS LEARNED

- Prefetch is an optimization that can become a liability for long-tail streaming workloads; optimistic parallelism needs explicit limits and signals.
- Feature flag rollouts touching cache invalidation should include streaming-specific canary traffic and automated rollback triggers tied to streaming health metrics.
- Observability: surface prefetch queue depth and lock contention metrics in the streaming dashboard to accelerate triage next time.
- Client SDKs: invest in more forgiving resume timeouts for streaming sessions or better client-side backoff to avoid thundering reconnects.

OPEN QUESTIONS / UNCERTAINTIES

- How many other prefixes are configured with the same invalidation pattern? Could this happen outside this single prefix? (Follow-up: run sweep across rollout config.)
- Could a different prefetch strategy (LIFO vs FIFO) have reduced memory-pressure impact? (Research spike.)
- Is there a way to coordinate invalidation rollout velocity with runtime prefetch throttles automatically? (Product discussion)

APPENDIX: RAW SIGNALS / QUICK HITS

- p99 streaming latency (us-west1): baseline ~120ms -> 2.3s at peak
- Observed extra 5xx: +1.2% during window; ~75% of those were edge 502/503, remainder server-side 504
- Prefetch queue depth: instrumented after incident showed peaks ~48 concurrent prefetch tasks for the hot prefix (we didn't have alerting at the time)
- Runtime switch used in mitigation: prefetch.mode=shallow-sync (temporary)
- Feature flag toggled: rollout-invalidation-prefix-A -> OFF at 17:21:02
- Related Jira: JIRA-INC-5421 (incident), JIRA-OPS-7823 (prefetch throttle story)

NOTES TO FUTURE-ONCALL

- If you see a p99 streaming jump without traffic increase, check invalidation rate by prefix immediately before assuming autoscaler issues.
- Have the feature flag CLI snippet ready in runbook; toggling invalidations can be the fastest stop-gap.
- Prefer toggling runtime prefetch to shallow mode rather than scaling GPUs—scaling doesn't address lock contention.

SESSION NOTES (oncall freeform)

- Marco: prefetch trace made it obvious quickly once we captured kernel stack—nice work.
- Evelyn: dashboard gap slowed root cause; prioritizing that now.
- Diego: rollout checklist will include 5 streaming-specific checks and a hold window.
- Priya: runtime lock work is non-trivial; we'll scope a quick-win (shallow deserialization) vs full redesign.

END

(Blameless, factual, next-steps prioritized)
